title: Notion vs Obsidian vs Coda for Solo Founders (2026) - The Real AI Operator
text:
## The 30-second version

- Pick Notion if you want one place for docs, tasks, CRM, and a wiki. It’s cloud-only, and per-seat pricing adds up the second you bring in collaborators. I use it every day, for what that’s worth.
- Pick Obsidian if you write a lot and your notes are how you think. Everything lives on your own machine. No subscription, no lock-in, no third party deciding whether you still have access tomorrow.
- Pick Coda if ops is what’s eating your week. It turns pipelines, trackers, and internal tools into docs you can maintain without paging a developer.

...

Viewers and editors are free. ... The free plan is unlimited for viewers and capped at a small number of Doc Makers.

...

| Feature | Notion | Obsidian | Coda |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Storage model | Cloud-only | Local Markdown files | Cloud (with offline editing) |
| Best for | Docs + tasks + wiki in one | Thinking, writing, knowledge base | Operations, trackers, internal tools |
| Pricing entry point | Free / Plus $12 per user per month | Free / Sync $4 per user per month | Free / Pro $10 per Doc Maker per month |
| Offline mode | Limited (recent pages only) | Full. It is a desktop app | Partial (edits sync when reconnected) |
| Database / tables | Yes (six view types) | Via plugins (Dataview) | Yes (the core feature) |
| Automations | Built-in (Notion Automations) | Via plugins | Built-in (Buttons + Packs) |
| AI features | Notion AI on every paid plan | Via plugins (Copilot, Smart Connections) | Coda Brain included on Pro |
| Public sharing | Yes (with Notion Sites) | Yes (with Publish add-on) | Yes (free) |
| Mobile apps | iOS, Android | iOS, Android (free; Sync is the paid add-on) | iOS, Android |
| Open data export | CSV / Markdown export | Already Markdown (yours forever) | CSV / Doc export |
| Learning curve | Medium (1-2 weeks) | Low for notes, high for plugin setup | Medium-high (it is a builder) |

One row worth flagging: storage model. Local Markdown means your notes sit on your disk forever, even if Obsidian the company disappears tomorrow. Cloud-only means you don’t think about backups, but you’re trusting someone else to keep the lights on. Not right or wrong, just a tradeoff you should pick on purpose.

...

...

### Writing your weekly investor update

Obsidian wins this one for people who think by writing. The weekly update is mostly prose, and Obsidian’s `[[link]]` syntax lets you reference a customer or a metric from any past note without leaving the keyboard. The reason it works: it’s a native desktop app reading and writing plain markdown files. No page reloads, no block-by-block loading. Notion handles it fine but those reloads interrupt long-form flow in a way a native app does not. Coda is the worst pick here because buttons and tables crowd the writing surface.

### Tracking investor pipeline and follow-ups

Coda wins this. A Coda CRM can pull in emails through the Gmail pack, set reminders, and fire off Slack notifications when a deal sits untouched for a week. The button-and-formula model is overkill for a simple contact list, but it’s exactly right for a pipeline with stages. Notion is a close second and has nicer templates out of the box. Obsidian is the wrong tool for CRM work in 2026 unless you enjoy maintaining plugins on a Friday night.

...

## Pricing for a one-person company

What you pay boils down to two things: how many people touch the workspace and which features you actually use. Here’s what a solo founder sees in August 2026.

- Notion: Free for personal use. Plus runs $10 per member per month on annual billing ($12 if you go monthly). Most solo folks stay on Free until they hit the file upload cap or need longer page history.
- Obsidian: The desktop app is free on every platform. If you want your iPad and phone to stay in sync, add Obsidian Sync at $4 a month, billed annually.
- Coda: Free for unlimited viewers. Pro is $10 per Doc Maker per month on annual billing. Most solo founders stick with Free because there’s only one of you editing.

The catch nobody mentions upfront: Notion bills per member, including people who just read. Coda bills per Doc Maker. So if you share your workspace with five advisors who only read, Notion charges you for six seats. Coda charges you for one. I set up a Notion workspace for a client a while back and handed out a few guest logins without thinking too hard about it. The bill at the end of the month made me wince.

Flip the math to a 20-person team and it reverses. Notion’s flat per-seat pricing usually beats Coda’s free-viewer play once everyone’s actively editing. So don’t pick on pricing alone. Look at who’s actually writing in the doc versus who’s just lurking.

...

## What I’d pick if I were starting over today

For a solo founder starting from scratch, no cofounder, no team, just you and the work, I’d start with Notion Free. It’s what I use for my own company wiki, CRM, and task board. Day-one basics for a one-person company, and Notion ships them out of the box.

When thinking work starts crowding out the operations stuff, research, interview transcripts, half-formed ideas you’d never put in a wiki, that’s when I’d add Obsidian on the side. What I saw going through the docs and community threads: it’s local-first, files are plain markdown, no lock-in. That second part matters more than people realize. If you ever want to bail, your notes are just .md files on disk. Notion handles the structured deliverables. Obsidian handles the thinking. They don’t compete. Tradeoff: cross-device sync isn’t free, and the plugin setup has a learning curve. For a founder buried in notes though, it earns its keep.

Once you’ve got a real team and ops starts eating your week, then I’d look at Coda for the internal tools. Solo, it’s overkill. The bill climbs fast. Notion + Obsidian is the lighter stack until then.

### 1. Coda — The Programmable Document Engine

Coda looks like Notion on the surface, but underneath, it behaves much more like a custom application builder.

- What Stands Out: Coda’s formula language is significantly more powerful than Notion’s rollups and formulas. You can drop interactive buttons into docs that trigger multi-step automations, query live APIs via Coda Packs, and calculate complex spreadsheet-grade formulas directly in paragraph text.
- The Trade-Off: The mobile app feels slightly heavier to navigate, and very large documents can take longer to initialize than simple markdown notes.
- Pricing Model Advantage: Coda charges only for Doc Makers (editors who create docs), while general team members who view or edit existing pages are completely free.

...

### 3. Obsidian — The Privacy-First Knowledge Base

For operators who want complete control over their internal notes without cloud subscription fees or proprietary lock-in, Obsidian stores everything as standard `.md` Markdown files directly on your local hard drive.

- What Stands Out: Instant search speed, an enormous community plugin library, bidirectional graph linking, and full offline functionality.
- The Trade-Off: Multi-user real-time collaboration requires setting up Obsidian Sync or private Git repositories; it lacks multi-user simultaneous real-time cursors.
- Pricing Check: See the official Obsidian pricing page.

## My Decision Framework: When Should You Leave Notion?

Here is my direct recommendation on when to switch:

1. Switch to Coda if: You find Notion’s databases too static and want interactive buttons, automations, and formulas that behave like bespoke internal software tools.
2. Switch to ClickUp if: Your team is missing deadlines because Notion lacks native time tracking, subtask dependencies, and workload capacity planning.
3. Switch to Obsidian if: You want 100% offline access, zero recurring cloud fees, and standard Markdown file portability.
4. Switch to Craft if: You are an Apple-centric agency that frequently shares polished client proposals and meeting decks.

title: Second Brain Tools 2026: Notion vs Obsidian for SMBs
text:
## Comparison at a glance

| Tool | Price range | Key feature | Who it’s for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Notion | $0-$20/user/month (paid tiers), AI add-on priced separately | Databases + docs + AI search in one workspace | Teams that want a single hub for docs, wikis, and project tracking |
| Obsidian | $0 personal use; $4-$10/user/month for Sync/Publish add-ons | Local-first markdown files with bidirectional linking | Teams that want full data ownership and a durable, tool-independent archive |
| Logseq | Free (open source); optional paid sync | Outliner-style daily notes with block references | Small teams or solo operators who think in daily logs |
| Coda (brief mention) | Pricing in flux amid a 2026 rebrand | Doc-plus-spreadsheet hybrid | Teams already invested in Coda’s existing workspace |

Prices above are ranges as of 2026 and vary by plan tier, seat count, and add-ons; confirm current pricing directly with each vendor before budgeting.

## Notion

Notion is the closest thing to an all-in-one workspace: docs, databases, wikis, and lightweight project tracking live in the same app, and pages can be linked and nested into a structure that mirrors how a team actually organizes itself. Notion AI v2 extends this by letting users query across a workspace in natural language and draft or summarize content directly inside pages, which shortens the gap between “we wrote this down somewhere” and “I found it.”

Strengths include a low learning curve for non-technical staff, flexible database views (table, board, calendar, gallery) that suit different workflows, and strong template availability for SOPs, onboarding docs, and client trackers. The tradeoff is that Notion’s flexibility can turn into workspace sprawl: without someone enforcing structure, pages multiply and search quality degrades. Notion is also a hosted, proprietary format, so exporting a fully faithful copy of a complex workspace for backup or migration takes more effort than a plain-text system.

Notion suits small business teams that want one shared home for both operational knowledge and lightweight project management, and that are willing to assign someone to keep the workspace organized as it grows.

## Obsidian

Obsidian takes a different approach: notes are stored as local markdown files, and the app’s core strength is bidirectional linking, connecting a decision to the client note it relates to, or a process doc to the tool it references, then visualizing those connections. Obsidian 1.8 improved the canvas feature for mapping out relationships and workflows visually, which is useful for documenting how processes actually connect rather than just listing them.

Because notes are plain markdown files on disk (or in your own cloud storage of choice), Obsidian gives a business full ownership of its knowledge archive with no vendor lock-in; the files remain readable and portable even if you stop paying for the app entirely.

Data portability is the standout benefit, backed by a highly capable free tier for individuals and a plugin ecosystem that lets teams extend functionality (task management, kanban boards, spaced repetition for training material) without waiting on the vendor. The learning curve is steeper than Notion’s, especially for non-technical staff, and native real-time multi-user collaboration is more limited; teams generally need the paid Sync add-on and some workflow discipline to avoid conflicting edits.

The best fit is a business that prioritizes long-term data ownership and wants a knowledge base that will outlast any single vendor, provided at least one team member is comfortable setting up structure and conventions for others to follow.

...

Coda offered a similar doc-plus-database hybrid to Notion, but is currently mid-rebrand following a 2026 acquisition, and its naming and product direction are unsettled; teams already using Coda should watch for official guidance before making further investment, and teams starting fresh may want to wait for the dust to settle before choosing it as a new system.

...

### Is Notion or Obsidian better for a small business?

Notion generally suits teams that want an all-in-one hub with easier real-time collaboration and lower onboarding friction. Obsidian generally suits teams that prioritize data ownership, portability, and a durable archive that isn’t tied to one vendor’s pricing or continuity. The right choice depends on your team’s collaboration style and technical comfort more than on raw feature count.

...

For most growing SMBs, the decision comes down to Notion versus Obsidian: Notion for an easier-to-adopt, collaboration-friendly hub with AI-assisted search built in, or Obsidian for a durable, fully-owned archive that stays useful even if you switch tools later. Logseq is worth a look for teams that prefer a daily-log workflow, and Coda is worth watching rather than adopting fresh while its rebrand plays out. Whichever system you choose, the tool matters less than whether someone owns keeping it organized. A second brain only works if the business actually uses it.

title: Notion vs Obsidian vs Coda: Who Actually Holds Your Data?
text:
Obsidian stores your notes as plain Markdown files in a folder on your own disk. That's the whole design, and it's a real advantage: your data isn't in anyone's cloud by default, "backing up" is just copying a folder, and if Obsidian vanished tomorrow your notes would open in any text editor. On pure ownership, nothing here beats it.

The trade-off is capability. Obsidian isn't a relational-database tool the way Notion is — its databases are lighter, collaboration isn't its strength, and sync across devices is a paid add-on rather than the default. You own everything; you just have less of the connected-database machinery that pulls people into Notion in the first place.

...

Notion is the opposite trade. Relational databases, rollups, formulas, real-time collaboration, a shared team workspace — genuinely powerful, and all of it lives on Notion's servers. You don't have a local copy, and the built-in export is lossy: relations flatten to text, rollups and formulas save frozen values, and views are dropped entirely (the full list of what's missing). So the more you build in Notion, the more capability you get — and the wider the gap between "my data" and "a copy I actually hold." Notion doesn't back it up for you, either; version history and Trash are safety nets on Notion's clock, not an off-site copy.

title: 8 Notion Alternatives in 2026, Priced Against Notion's $20 AI
text:
## 2. Coda (Now Superhuman Docs): Closest All-in-One Replacement

Best for: teams that love Notion’s docs-plus-databases idea but need more powerful tables, formulas and automations.

Coda was renamed Superhuman Docs on July 8, 2026, after Grammarly, which owns Coda, renamed itself Superhuman. Most people still search for it as Coda. The product and your existing docs carry on. It mixes documents, tables, buttons and automations, and its tables behave more like a real database than Notion’s.

Pricing: free plan available. Pro is $12 per Doc Maker per month billed yearly ($15 monthly), up from $10, and Business (formerly Team) is $33 yearly ($40 monthly), up from $30. Only Doc Makers (people who create docs) are billed; editors and viewers are free. That can make it much cheaper than Notion for a team where one or two people build and everyone else just uses the docs.

If you already pay for Coda: Superhuman says existing customers keep their current plan and price. Upgrading your plan moves you onto the new Superhuman pricing, so check before you change tiers. See Superhuman’s Coda billing help page.

Security: Coda has long been SOC 2 Type 2 certified, and that carries over under Superhuman.

- More powerful tables, formulas and buttons than Notion
- Pay only for the people who create docs
- Integrations (“Packs”) pull data in from other tools

- List prices rose with the Superhuman rebrand
- Steeper learning curve for advanced features
- Fewer templates and a smaller community than Notion

Coda vs Notion: the closest like-for-like switch. Pick it if you want Notion’s flexibility with stronger data tools.

## 3. Obsidian: Best for Private Notes

Best for: freelancers, writers and researchers who want fast, private notes they fully own.

Obsidian stores every note as a plain Markdown file on your own device. There’s no cloud account required, it works fully offline, and if Obsidian disappeared tomorrow you would still have your notes as normal text files. Links between notes and the graph view make it excellent for building a personal knowledge base.

Since 2025 it also has Bases, a core feature that turns notes into table views you can filter and sort, using each note’s properties as columns. It’s useful for reading lists, client notes or simple trackers, though it’s newer and less powerful than Notion’s databases.

Pricing: free for personal and work use. Obsidian dropped its required commercial license in 2025, and businesses can buy one optionally to support development. Sync costs $4 per month billed yearly ($5 monthly) to keep notes in step across devices, and Publish costs $8 per site per month billed yearly. See Obsidian’s pricing page.

- Completely private and offline
- Very fast, even with thousands of notes
- Huge plugin library, including AI plugins

- Bases table views are newer and less powerful than Notion’s databases
- Weak for team collaboration
- Plugins mean more setup and maintenance

Obsidian vs Notion: better for one person’s notes and writing. Not a team workspace.
